title: Where to Stay in Seoul: Myeongdong, Hongdae, Gangnam, and Other Neighborhoods Compared
html:
One of the biggest questions first-time visitors have isn't "what should I see in Seoul?" — it's "where should I actually sleep?" Seoul is huge, and picking a hotel or guesthouse in the wrong area can mean an extra 40 minutes on the subway every single day. The good news: Seoul's subway system connects almost everywhere, so you're rarely "stuck." Still, some neighborhoods make your trip much easier than others, especially if this is your first time in Korea. Here's an honest, beginner-friendly comparison of the areas foreign travelers ask about most.

Myeongdong — classic, central, and easy for first-timers

Myeongdong (명동) is Seoul's best-known shopping district, packed with cosmetics stores, street food carts, and department stores. It's one of the most popular places for first-time visitors to stay, mainly because it's so central — you're a short subway ride from Gyeongbokgung Palace, Namsan Tower, and City Hall.

  • Typical hotel price: approx. 80,000–180,000 KRW a night for a mid-range hotel room
  • Getting around: served by Myeongdong Station (Line 4) and Euljiro 1-ga Station (Line 2)
  • Good for: first-timers who want convenience and don't mind crowds


Myeongdong's main shopping street stays busy well into the evening. Photo: ProjectManhattan, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The trade-off: Myeongdong is very touristy, so restaurants there are often priced for visitors rather than locals, and it can feel more like a shopping mall than a "real" neighborhood at night. If you want a quieter home base, keep reading.

Hongdae — nightlife, indie culture, and budget-friendly stays

Hongdae (홍대) is the area around Hongik University, known for live music clubs, street performances, and a young, artsy crowd. It's a favorite with budget travelers and anyone who wants to be near Seoul's nightlife without paying Gangnam prices.

  • Typical hotel/guesthouse price: approx. 40,000–100,000 KRW a night, including plenty of hostel and guesthouse options
  • Getting around: served by Hongik University Station (Line 2, and the AREX airport train)
  • Good for: budget travelers, younger travelers, anyone prioritizing nightlife and cafés


A street in Hongdae, lined with cafés, shops, and small clubs. Photo: U0894629, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

One nice bonus: because Hongik University Station is on the AREX (Airport Railroad Express) line, Hongdae can be an easy first or last stop if you're flying in or out of Incheon Airport with heavy luggage.

Itaewon — international food, bars, and an expat-friendly feel

Itaewon (이태원) is Seoul's most international neighborhood, historically shaped by the nearby US military base and now home to a large expat and immigrant community. If you're craving something other than Korean food, or want bars with a more international crowd, this is the area.

  • Typical hotel price: approx. 70,000–150,000 KRW a night
  • Getting around: served by Itaewon Station (Line 6)
  • Good for: foodies who want variety, LGBTQ+ travelers (Itaewon has Seoul's main gay nightlife strip), and anyone who wants a less "purely touristy" home base


Seoul Central Mosque, a long-standing landmark in Itaewon that reflects the neighborhood's international character. Photo: Republic of Korea (Korea.net), CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

A respectful note: in October 2022, a tragic crowd crush during Halloween celebrations happened near Itaewon Station, and the neighborhood has since put more crowd-safety measures in place for busy nights. It's still a completely normal, welcoming area to stay in — just be mindful of crowd size if you're out during a major holiday weekend.

Gangnam — modern, upscale, and business-oriented

Gangnam (강남, literally "south of the river") is Seoul's modern business and shopping district, full of glass office towers, luxury department stores, and the COEX underground mall. It's clean, efficient, and very safe — but it's also further from most of the historic sights, which are mostly north of the Han River.

  • Typical hotel price: approx. 100,000–250,000 KRW a night, often more for well-known international hotel brands
  • Getting around: served by Gangnam Station and Yeoksam Station (Line 2)
  • Good for: business travelers, K-pop and modern-shopping fans, travelers who don't mind a longer ride to the palaces and old town


A view over the Gangnam district, Seoul's modern business and shopping hub. Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

For a first trip, most guides (including this one) recommend basing yourself north of the river instead — but if your trip is more about shopping, K-pop culture, or business, Gangnam makes a lot of sense.

Bukchon & Ikseon-dong — traditional hanok charm

If you'd rather sleep inside a piece of Korean history, look at Bukchon Hanok Village and neighboring Ikseon-dong, both near Anguk Station. A hanok (한옥) is a traditional Korean house with a tiled or thatched roof and a small courtyard — dozens have been converted into boutique guesthouses here.

  • Typical hanok guesthouse price: approx. 90,000–200,000 KRW a night, since rooms are usually limited
  • Getting around: served by Anguk Station (Line 3), walking distance to Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces
  • Good for: travelers who want atmosphere over convenience, and don't mind smaller rooms or shared bathrooms


Bukchon-ro 11-gil, one of the most photographed streets in Bukchon Hanok Village. Photo: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Because these are real, small residential streets, please keep your voice down early in the morning and late at night — actual families still live in many of these houses.

How Koreans actually think about this

Ask a Korean friend where to stay, and they'll rarely say Myeongdong — it's seen as a place to shop, not somewhere locals would choose to sleep. When Koreans from other cities visit Seoul, they tend to pick a neighborhood based on what they're doing that trip: somewhere near Hongdae or Seongsu-dong for a fun weekend with friends, somewhere near Gangnam for business, or they simply stay with family. As a foreign visitor, though, you don't have that flexibility — so leaning toward a well-connected, central area (Myeongdong, or Bukchon/Ikseon-dong if you want more atmosphere) is still the safer beginner choice.

So which one should you pick?

If this is your first trip and you want the least stressful option, Myeongdong is hard to beat. If you're on a budget or want nightlife, go with Hongdae. Want variety in food and a more international feel? Try Itaewon. Traveling for shopping, K-pop, or business? Gangnam makes sense. And if you want your hotel itself to feel like part of the sightseeing, look at Bukchon or Ikseon-dong.

Quick comparison: Seoul neighborhoods for first-time visitors

Area Price range (per night) Subway access Vibe Best for
Myeongdong 80,000–180,000 KRW Excellent (Lines 2, 4) Busy shopping district First-timers, convenience
Hongdae 40,000–100,000 KRW Excellent (Line 2, AREX) Youthful, artsy, nightlife Budget travelers, nightlife fans
Itaewon 70,000–150,000 KRW Good (Line 6) International, diverse Foodies, LGBTQ+ travelers
Gangnam 100,000–250,000 KRW Excellent (Line 2) Modern, upscale, corporate Shopping, K-pop, business
Bukchon / Ikseon-dong 90,000–200,000 KRW Good (Line 3) Traditional, quiet, atmospheric Culture lovers, romantic trips

💬 Still torn between two of these areas? Tell me what your trip is mainly about (food, nightlife, shopping, or sightseeing) in the comments — happy to help you decide!
meta_description: A beginner's comparison of Seoul neighborhoods for first-time visitors: Myeongdong, Hongdae, Itaewon, Gangnam, and Bukchon, with prices, subway access, and who each area suits best.
